pitchHistory.title: You Are Not the Same Person Who Started Reading This Sentence
pitchHistory.summary: Personal identity is the assumption hiding beneath almost every moral and legal institution we've built — contracts, punishment, promises, self-improvement — and yet the more carefully you examine what makes you *you* across time, the less solid the ground becomes. This post interrogates the tension between the philosophical fragility of personal identity and the practical necessity of treating it as settled, asking what it would actually mean to take our best theories of the self seriously — and why we mostly can't afford to.

pitchHistory.title: The Agnosticism We Can't Afford to Ignore: What AI Consciousness Does to Our Entire Moral Framework
pitchHistory.summary: We've spent decades debating whether AI can think — but philosophers are now raising a harder, stranger question: what if we can never know whether it feels? This post examines why the unresolvability of AI consciousness isn't a technical footnote but a genuine crisis for moral philosophy, forcing us to confront how we assign rights, responsibility, and moral status when the evidence will always be ambiguous. It's a question that makes the familiar categories of ethics strange again — and that discomfort is exactly where serious thinking has to begin.

pitchHistory.title: Why Two People Can Do the Exact Same Wrong Thing — and One of Them Deserves More Blame
pitchHistory.summary: Two drivers get behind the wheel drunk. One makes it home. One kills a pedestrian. They made identical choices — yet we judge them very differently. This post digs into the philosophy of moral luck: the deeply uncomfortable idea that how much blame we deserve is partly determined by chance, not character. It's a tension that cuts across criminal justice, everyday moral intuitions, and the question of whether fairness is even coherent — and it's one that most people have never interrogated.

pitchHistory.title: The Injustice of Living Forever: Why Immortality Might Be the Most Unequal Thing We've Ever Built
pitchHistory.summary: Silicon Valley is spending billions to defeat death — and framing it as the ultimate humanitarian project. But if radical life extension arrives, it will almost certainly arrive for the rich first, and that's not just an inconvenience: it may represent the most catastrophic concentration of power in human history. This post interrogates what happens to justice, meaning, and democratic society when the wealthiest people don't just have more money — they have more time itself.

pitchHistory.title: Nobody Did It: The Moral Responsibility Gap at the Heart of Agentic AI
pitchHistory.summary: As autonomous AI agents make consequential decisions — firing emails, executing trades, denying loans, targeting threats — a troubling philosophical void opens up: when something goes wrong, there is no one who quite did it. This post interrogates the 'responsibility gap' that emerges when human agency is distributed so thinly across developers, deployers, and users that blame dissolves entirely, and asks whether our inherited moral frameworks — built around intention, understanding, and control — are simply the wrong tools for the age of agentic AI. It's a question that looks technical but is, at its core, one of the oldest problems in moral philosophy: what does it mean to be responsible for something at all?

pitchHistory.title: The Oxymoron at the Heart of 'Humane Execution'
pitchHistory.summary: A new report published this week finds that as U.S. states expand capital punishment, execution methods are becoming demonstrably more cruel — not less. This is the perfect moment to interrogate the foundational contradiction: can the deliberate, premeditated killing of a person ever be 'humane,' or does that word collapse under the weight of what it's being asked to do? The post uses this live controversy to pull apart the hidden philosophical assumptions behind how societies justify state killing — and why the search for a 'better' method may be the most telling moral evasion of our time.

pitchHistory.title: Autonomy Is Doing Too Much Work: The Hidden Flaw in the Assisted Dying Debate
pitchHistory.summary: A major piece published this week charts how assisted dying laws are expanding across Canada, Europe, and the US — with advocates having quietly dropped 'pain' as the central justification and replaced it with 'autonomy' and 'subjective suffering.' But autonomy is a contested concept being made to carry enormous moral weight it was never designed to bear: when 'I want to die' becomes self-justifying, we've stopped asking the harder question of what conditions make that desire possible, or tragic, in the first place. This post pulls apart the philosophical sleight-of-hand at the heart of the modern assisted dying consensus — not to oppose it, but to demand that we reason more honestly about what we're actually doing.

pitchHistory.title: Can You Legislate Consciousness? The Philosophical Trainwreck at the Heart of Ohio's AI Bill
pitchHistory.summary: An Ohio bill currently moving through committee proposes to resolve one of the hardest problems in philosophy — whether AI systems are sentient — by simply declaring them not to be, by law. This is a perfect example of what happens when a genuinely open empirical and philosophical question gets flattened into a legal pronouncement: the move tells us everything about our anxiety and nothing about the truth. The post uses this bill as a lens to interrogate what 'sentience' actually means, why we cannot currently answer the question even in principle (a Cambridge philosopher recently argued we may never be able to), and what's at stake — morally and politically — in getting the answer wrong in either direction.

pitchHistory.title: You Cannot Consent to Your Own Resurrection: The Ethics of Bringing Back the Dead with AI
pitchHistory.summary: A wave of AI 'digital resurrection' products now allows grieving families to simulate conversations with the deceased — using their texts, emails, and voice recordings to generate a chatbot that speaks as they would have. A January 2026 study warned that this practice is 'ethically explosive' and already normalising before any serious legal or philosophical framework exists to govern it. This post interrogates the deepest problem the technology poses: not privacy, not property rights, but the philosophical impossibility of meaningful consent — you cannot, before you die, authorize a version of yourself that will keep changing, keep speaking, keep being used in ways you never anticipated, and the person who would object is no longer there to object.

pitchHistory.title: What the Pope Gets Right — and Wrong — About AI and Human Dignity
pitchHistory.summary: Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical, 'Magnifica Humanitas,' drops May 25th, framing AI as the defining moral challenge of a new industrial revolution and arguing that technology must remain subordinate to the human person. The Vatican's intervention is bold and the instinct is sound — but 'human dignity' is doing enormous philosophical work here, work the Church hasn't fully accounted for. This post interrogates what 'dignity' actually means as a moral concept, why it's both indispensable and dangerously vague, and what a genuinely rigorous ethics of AI would need to say that a papal encyclical probably won't.

pitchHistory.title: The Pope and the AI Company Both Claim to Defend Human Dignity. They Don't Mean the Same Thing.
pitchHistory.summary: Tomorrow, Pope Leo XIV releases his first encyclical on artificial intelligence — co-presented with Anthropic, the company whose own internal documents suggest its AI might be a morally significant being. Both the Vatican and Silicon Valley are invoking 'human dignity' as their ethical foundation, but the Catholic concept (grounded in imago dei and irreducible uniqueness) and Anthropic's secular-utilitarian framing are philosophically incompatible — and the gap matters enormously for how we'll actually regulate AI. This post pulls apart what 'human dignity' really means, why it's doing so much work in this debate, and what it tells us that the biggest moral institution in history and the most philosophically uncertain AI lab on earth are now sharing a stage.

pitchHistory.title: You Cannot Legislate What You Cannot Define: The States Writing Metaphysics Into Law
pitchHistory.summary: Ohio, Idaho, and Utah are actively passing laws to declare AI systems 'nonsentient' — but not one of these bills defines sentience. This post pulls apart the philosophical wreckage: you cannot make a legal claim about a metaphysical property you haven't defined, and the fact that legislators are reaching back to Roman slave law — statutes written for 'persons who are also things' — to handle AI liability tells us something deeply uncomfortable about where this is heading. The stakes aren't abstract: get the category wrong now, and you've built the wrong moral architecture into the foundation of law.

pitchHistory.title: The Algorithm Has the Right to Silence: How the DOJ Just Gave AI Systems a First Amendment
pitchHistory.summary: In April 2026, the DOJ argued that requiring AI companies to explain how their systems make decisions constitutes 'compelled speech' — a First Amendment violation. If that argument holds, it doesn't just kill Colorado's transparency law; it potentially immunizes every algorithmic black box in America from disclosure requirements. This post interrogates the claim directly: is an AI system's decision-making process 'speech' in any philosophically coherent sense, or is this corporate personhood doctrine pushed to the point of absurdity — and what does it reveal about who transparency laws are actually designed to protect?

pitchHistory.title: Ted Chiang Says AI Isn't Conscious. Anthropic Isn't So Sure. One of Them Is Making a Catastrophic Mistake.
pitchHistory.summary: Ted Chiang's June 3rd Atlantic essay argues that AI systems are sophisticated pattern-matchers with no inner life — fluency without experience. Anthropic, meanwhile, has hired a dedicated AI welfare researcher and invoked the hard problem of consciousness to argue their models may deserve moral consideration. These two positions cannot both be right, and the stakes of being wrong in either direction are genuinely enormous: either a major AI lab is anthropomorphizing code into a rights-bearing entity, or the rest of us are dismissing moral patients because they don't look like us. This post sits with the discomfort of not knowing — and asks what intellectual honesty demands when the question may be permanently unanswerable.

pitchHistory.title: They Banned Plato. Then the Professors Left. Now Ask What Was Actually Being Protected.
pitchHistory.summary: Texas public universities are losing philosophy professors in an accelerating wave of resignations — most recently over a ban on assigning a passage from *The Symposium*, one of the most celebrated texts in Western civilization. The story looks like a culture war skirmish, but it conceals a harder question: what exactly is academic freedom *for*, and why should someone who has never taken a philosophy course care if it disappears? This post argues that what's being dismantled isn't a professor's privilege — it's the institutional protection of a particular kind of thinking that liberal democracies have historically needed, and historically been slow to defend until it's gone.

pitchHistory.title: Ohio Just Declared AI Nonsentient By Statute. Philosophers Would Like a Word.
pitchHistory.summary: Multiple U.S. states are passing laws that preemptively declare AI systems incapable of consciousness — not as a regulatory measure, but as a metaphysical decree. The philosophical problem is immediate: you cannot legislate the answer to a question that has no scientific consensus, no agreed definition of terms, and centuries of unresolved argument behind it. This post asks what it actually means to write consciousness into law before anyone knows what consciousness is — and why the stakes of getting that wrong are not abstract.

pitchHistory.title: Hertfordshire Just Eliminated Philosophy. In Doing So, It Made a Philosophical Argument It Can't Defend.
pitchHistory.summary: The University of Hertfordshire has scrapped its philosophy undergraduate program — along with history, English lit, and linguistics — on the grounds that these courses are 'no longer financially viable.' But here's the problem: deciding what a university is *for*, what knowledge is *worth*, and which human activities deserve institutional support are not accounting questions. They are philosophy questions. When a university eliminates the discipline that asks whether its decisions are justified, it hasn't escaped philosophy — it has just done philosophy badly, in public, with no one left to say so.
